books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

stimulus.text: Senator Huey Long of Louisiana, photographed in 1935 seated at a desk in front of shelves of law books, gesturing with both hands as he speaks. Long built a national following with his Share Our Wealth program, which proposed capping large fortunes and guaranteeing every family a homestead and a minimum income.
stimulus.source_note: Huey Long at desk, 1935 press photograph. Public domain; via Wikimedia Commons.

source: original; stimulus photograph by an unknown press photographer, 1935, public domain
stem: Long's movement and the American Liberty League are best compared as

options.text: Allies who both wanted Roosevelt reelected in 1936
options.misconception: The Liberty League denounced Roosevelt as a socialist, while Long attacked him for doing too little; neither was an ally.

options.text: Movements both funded by large corporate donors
options.misconception: Corporate money backed the Liberty League, while Long attacked large fortunes and drew on ordinary followers.

options.text: Movements that both wanted the New Deal repealed
options.misconception: Long wanted the New Deal to go further, not to be repealed; repeal was the conservatives' aim.

options.text: Opposite pressures on Roosevelt, for more and for less

rationales.A: Background from the books: the Liberty League called Roosevelt a socialist and Long called him too cautious, so neither backed his reelection as an ally.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the Liberty League drew on Du Pont money, while Long's clubs were a mass following of ordinary people.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Long wanted more redistribution, not repeal; only the League's side wanted the New Deal rolled back.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the books place Long on the left demanding more and the League on the right demanding less, squeezing Roosevelt from both sides.
rationales.general:
1. Long demanded that government do more to share wealth.
2. The Liberty League demanded that government do less and leave business alone.
3. Both were attacks on Roosevelt, but from opposite directions.
4. So the two movements are best read as opposite pressures, not as allies.
Remember: two critics of the same president can want opposite things; compare their demands, not their target.
